note.question: When should competing commodity importers use contingent rather than fixed procurement prices, and can volatile index-linked prices improve responsiveness or soften downstream quantity competition?
note.overview: Two competing importers simultaneously select contingent-price or fixed-price sourcing contracts and then play a Bayesian Cournot quantity game after observing correlated private demand signals. The paper solves the unique continuation equilibrium in every contract subgame and characterizes first-stage sourcing equilibria.

components.label: Model sequence and system structure
components.explanation: At sourcing time Ts, firms A and B simultaneously choose CPC or FPC while knowing the fixed price and the distributions of demand and the future CPC price. At ordering time To, each privately observes a noisy demand signal and simultaneously chooses an order quantity, updating both demand and—under CPC—the procurement price. At delivery time Td, demand and the CPC price realize, the firms receive their orders, and they sell in the local Cournot market. CPC and FPC choices determine which procurement costs remain uncertain and therefore which dimensions each signal updates.

components.label: Sourcing Nash equilibrium with unique Bayesian Cournot continuation equilibria
components.explanation: The model's equilibrium concept is Sourcing Nash equilibrium with unique Bayesian Cournot continuation equilibria. Lemma 2 establishes a unique Bayesian Nash equilibrium in every CPC/FPC continuation subgame. The ex ante equilibrium profits from those subgames determine first-stage best responses. Propositions 3-5 then characterize the Nash equilibria of the simultaneous sourcing game for zero versus positive demand-price correlation and equal versus unequal expected contract costs.
